title: Waiting for, proud of, used to: words with a fixed preposition
title_target: Du kan vara stolt över jobbet du har gjort.
goal: Use the most common Swedish verbs and adjectives together with the preposition they always bring along, even when English picks a different one.
bekal: you can say what you are waiting for, thinking about, longing for and depending on
you can talk about feelings with *rädd för*, *stolt över*, *nöjd med*, *orolig för*, *van vid*
you can put a preposition before *att* + verb, before an *att*-clause, and at the end of a question
wave: Go back to Unit 7 (Particle verbs II): say ten particle verbs aloud with the stress on the particle (*ta UPP*, *stänga AV*), then say *vänta på*, *titta på*, *prata om* with an unstressed preposition, and hear the difference.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vi väntar på Karin
dialogs.intro: Monday morning at the design agency in Göteborg. The team meeting should have started ten minutes ago, but Karin is not there yet. Dian and Mattias wait by the coffee machine; Dian is presenting to a client later today.

lines.text: Har du sett Karin? Vi har väntat på henne i tio minuter.

lines.literal: have you seen Karin? we have waited on her in ten minutes.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Hon ringde nyss. Bussen står still vid Järntorget, så vi får vänta lite till.

notes: **Vi har väntat på henne** — Swedish waits *on* someone (**på**), English waits *for* them. Swedish also has no continuous form, so *har väntat* covers both "have waited" and "have been waiting". The length of time takes **i**: *i tio minuter* (for ten minutes), as you saw in Svenska 102.

**Vad tänker du på?** — the preposition goes to the end of the question, exactly like English "What are you thinking about?". Say it **vah TENG-ker dü poh**, with *på* short and unstressed. Moving it to the front (*På vad tänker du?*) is not wrong, but it sounds like a nineteenth-century novel.

**Rädd för att göra bort mig** — where English uses a preposition + *-ing* ("afraid **of** embarrass**ing**"), Swedish uses a preposition + **att** + the base form: *rädd **för att** göra*. *Göra bort sig* is a reflexive particle verb meaning "to make a fool of oneself", pronounced **YÖ-rah boht say**.

**Jättenöjd med** — *nöjd* (pleased, satisfied) always takes **med**: *nöjd med skisserna*. The prefix *jätte-* (giant) is the everyday way to say "really, super": *jättebra*, *jättekul*, *jättenöjd* → **YET-teh-nöyd**.

**Intresserad av, stolt över** — two classic traps. English is interested *in*, Swedish is interested *of* (**av**); English is proud *of*, Swedish is proud *over* (**över**). *Intresserad i* is the single most common preposition mistake learners make, so say *intresserad av* aloud five times now.

**Allt beror på om…** — *bero på* means "to depend on": *Det beror på* (It depends). It also gives reasons: *Förseningen beror på snön* (The delay is due to the snow). *Trött på* is not just tired but fed up: *trött på bussarna* = sick of the buses.

grammars.title: Verbs that bring their own preposition
body: Some Swedish verbs almost never appear without a particular preposition. Learn them as a pair, the way you would learn *en* or *ett* with a noun: not *vänta* but *vänta på*, not *längta* but *längta efter*. The preposition is unstressed, and the object follows it.

head: Svenska
English
Example
rows: Jag tänker ofta på min familj.
Hon drömmer om ett eget företag.
Han bryr sig inte om pengar.

after: Watch **svara på**: English answers a question directly, Swedish answers *on* it: *svara **på** frågan*. Without *på*, *svara* only takes a person or nothing at all: *Hon svarade inte*.

**Tycka om** (like) looks like one of these, but it isn't: there *om* is a particle and carries the stress, **TÜK-kah OM**. Compare *prata om* (talk about), where *om* is an unstressed preposition. More on this in the second section.

grammars.title: What can follow the preposition
body: After a fixed preposition Swedish can put a noun or pronoun, **att** + the base form of a verb, a whole **att**-clause, or a clause beginning with **om** (whether) or a question word. English often needs an *-ing* form or a different construction.

head: English
Svenska
rows: Jag är rädd **för att göra** fel.
Hon är stolt **över att hon klarade** det.
It depends on whether it works.
We talked about what we should do.
Vi pratade **om vad** vi skulle göra.

after: In questions and relative clauses the preposition is left stranded at the end, as in English: *Vem väntar du **på**?* (Who are you waiting for?), *Det är något jag har tänkt **på*** (It's something I've been thinking about).

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Middag hos Oskars föräldrar
dialogs.intro: Sunday evening in Askim. Oskar's parents have invited Dian to dinner again, and this time his mother wants to hear everything about the internship.

lines.speaker: Oskars mamma:
lines.text: Vad roligt att du ville komma igen, Dian! Oskar säger att du har mycket att göra.
lines.id: How lovely that you wanted to come again, Dian! Oskar says you've got a lot on.
lines.literal: what fun that you wanted come again, Dian! Oskar says that you have much to do.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Tack för att jag fick komma. Jag har längtat efter riktig hemlagad mat.
lines.id: Thank you for having me. I've been longing for real home-cooked food.
lines.literal: thanks for that I got come. I have longed after real home-made food.

lines.speaker: Oskars mamma:
lines.text: Hur trivs du på jobbet? Är du nöjd med praktiken?
lines.id: How are you getting on at work? Are you happy with the internship?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Mycket. Jag är intresserad av UX-design, och det är precis vad vi jobbar med.

lines.text: Då har du all anledning att vara stolt över dig själv.

lines.text: Du är ju jättebra på det! Du är bara orolig för grammatiken.
lines.id: But you're really good at it! You're just worried about the grammar.

lines.id: Nobody cares about a few grammar mistakes. What matters is that people understand each other.

lines.text: Det har ni rätt i. Jag ska försöka tänka mindre på felen.
lines.id: You're right about that. I'll try to think less about the mistakes.

lines.text: Precis. Och nu: vem är sugen på efterrätt?

notes: **Längta efter** — to long for, to look forward to (something you miss): *Jag längtar efter sommaren*. The preposition is **efter** (after). Without an object, *längta hem* means "to be homesick", a phrase Dian knows only too well.

**Hur trivs du?** — *trivas* is an *-s* verb (like *hoppas* and *finnas*) meaning "to enjoy being somewhere, to feel at home". English has no single verb for it: *Jag trivs i Göteborg* = I like it here, I'm happy in Göteborg. Pronounced **TREE-vahs**, present tense *trivs* → **trivs**.

**Intresserad av** vs **intressera sig för** — the adjective takes **av**, but the reflexive verb takes **för**: *Hon är intresserad av design* = *Hon intresserar sig för design*. Same meaning, two different prepositions. Typically Swedish, and worth one extra minute.
**Van vid att prata** — *van vid* = used to, accustomed to. *Vid* is pronounced **veed**. Like *rädd för att*, it can be followed by **att** + base form: *Jag är van vid att gå upp tidigt*.

**Bra på, orolig för** — good *at* is *bra **på***, bad at is *dålig på*; worried *about* is *orolig **för***. And **sugen på** (craving, in the mood for) is one of the most useful words at a Swedish table: *Är du sugen på kaffe?*

**Det har ni rätt i** — the object *det* is fronted (you met this in Unit 3), so the verb comes next and the subject after it. *Ha rätt i något* = to be right about something. Dian uses *ni* because she is speaking to both Oskar and his mother.

grammars.title: Adjectives with a fixed preposition
body: Feelings and attitudes are mostly adjectives in Swedish, and each one comes with its own preposition. The adjective still agrees with the subject: *Han är nöjd*, *De är nöjd**a*** *med resultatet*.

head: Svenska
English
Example
rows: Jag är glad för din skull.
Hon är gift med en norrman.
Han är bra på att laga mat.
Hon är kär i sin granne.

after: Remember the plural *-a*: *vana*, *stolta*, *intresserade*, *trötta*. *Glad* has a useful split: *glad **över** något* (happy about something), *glad **för** någons skull* (happy for someone).

sections.title: Where Swedish and English part ways

blocks.text: Most of the time a Swedish preposition matches the English one closely enough: *prata om* (talk about), *titta på* (look at), *lyssna på* (listen to, literally "listen on"). The table below collects the pairs where the two languages disagree. These are the ones that give a learner away, so they deserve a sticky note on the fridge.

blocks.title: Three habits that help
items: Learn every new verb or adjective together with its preposition, and write it that way in your notebook: *nöjd med*, never just *nöjd*.
When in doubt in speech, **på** is the most frequent fixed preposition in Swedish. It is wrong often enough, but right more often than any other guess.
Collect whole sentences, not pairs: *Jag är inte van vid det än* sticks far better than *van vid = used to*.

sections.title: Particle or preposition? Listen to the stress

blocks.text: Swedish has two kinds of little words after verbs. A **preposition** is unstressed and simply links the verb to an object: *TITTA på tv*, *VÄNTA på bussen*. A **particle** is stressed and changes the meaning of the verb: *tycka OM* (to like), *ta UPP* (to bring up), as you practiced in Unit 7. Sometimes the very same verb + word means two different things depending on where the stress falls.

head: Unstressed (preposition)
Stressed (particle)
rows: *HÄLSA på grannen* = say hello to the neighbor
*PRATA om filmen* = talk about the film
*ta PÅ sig jackan* = put on the jacket

blocks.text: A practical test: if the little word can be dropped and the verb still means roughly the same (*vänta* / *vänta på*), it is a preposition. If dropping it changes the meaning completely (*tycka* = think, *tycka om* = like), it is a particle, and it takes the stress.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 12
items: Turn five sentences from this unit into cleft sentences with *det är … som*: *Det är Karin som vi väntar på.* *Det är appen som de är intresserade av.*
Notice that the preposition stays at the very end, after the verb, just like in a question.
Then do the same with *det var … som* in the past: *Det var bussarna som Karin var trött på.*
